concept.name: Risk parity
concept.definition: A portfolio construction approach that allocates so that each asset or asset class contributes equally to total portfolio volatility, rather than allocating equal capital. Its best-known form is the equally-weighted risk contributions portfolio; leveraged implementations (e.g. Bridgewater's 1996 All Weather fund) scale the balanced portfolio to a target return.
concept.intuition: A 60/40 stock-bond portfolio carries roughly 90% of its risk in stocks; risk parity rebalances so bonds, equities, and other assets each carry an equal share of the portfolio's ups and downs.
concept.mechanics: Given covariance matrix Sigma, portfolio volatility sigma(w) = sqrt(w' Sigma w) decomposes by Euler's theorem into per-asset risk contributions RC_i = w_i (Sigma w)_i / sigma(w); the ERC solution equalizes RC_i across all i, typically via convex optimization. Lower-risk assets receive larger capital weights, often topped up with leverage to reach return targets.
concept.formula: ERC condition: w_i * (Sigma w)_i = w_j * (Sigma w)_j for all i, j, i.e. RC_i = sigma(w) / N, with sigma(w) = sqrt(w' Sigma w) and Sigma the return covariance matrix.
concept.failure_modes: It depends on estimated volatilities and correlations; correlation regime shifts — stocks and bonds falling together, as in Q1 2020 or the 2022 tightening cycle — hit leveraged, bond-heavy allocations hard. The approach embeds leverage and duration risk, and its diversification premise fails exactly when cross-asset correlations jump toward one.
concept.misconceptions: Risk parity is not equal weights and not necessarily low risk: equalizing risk contributions usually requires levering the low-volatility assets, so the portfolio can carry substantial embedded leverage and interest-rate sensitivity.
concept.example: If equity volatility is 16% and bond volatility 6%, an unlevered two-asset risk-parity portfolio holds roughly 27% equities and 73% bonds so each side contributes half of portfolio volatility, versus 60/40 by capital.
